short: Fractographical characterization of hot pressed and pressure
title: Fractographical characterization of hot pressed and pressureless sintered AlN-doped ZrB2-SiC composites

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: ZrB2-SiC ultra-high-temperature ceramics need full densification without costly high-pressure hot pressing. How AlN doping changes the interfacial phases and the fracture mode of ZrB2-SiC is uncharacterised.
states.detail: Absorbed: m1 (HYP/need), m2 (HYP/gap), m3 (HYP/hypothesis), m4 (DES/base_system), m5 (DES/modification), m6 (DES/variable_sweep), m7 (PRC/forming), m8 (PRC/forming)

states.title: Structure state
states.head: AlN is fully consumed: HP5 holds BN and graphite, PS5 holds Al2OC; no AlN or Al2O3 reflections remain. Nano-scale Al-rich, N- and B-bearing glassy layers and a multilayer carbon band wet the ZrB2/SiC boundaries.
states.detail: Absorbed: m9 (STR/phase/identity), m10 (STR/interface), m11 (STR/microstructure/porosity), m12 (STR/microstructure/porosity). Premises: Reaction set: AlN + B2O3 -> BN + Al2O3; Al2O3 + SiO2 -> low-melting metakaolinite spinel; Al2O3 + C -> Al2OC + CO; Residual pyrolysis carbon graphitises at high temperature and pressure

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: Hot-pressed fracture is dominantly transgranular; pressureless samples fail intergranularly at necks. Vickers hardness peaks at 20.3 GPa for HP1 and falls to 6.8 GPa for PS5.
states.detail: Absorbed: m13 (PRP/behavior_class), m14 (PRP/value), m15 (MEC/pathway), m16 (MEC/tradeoff). Premises: Reaction set: AlN + B2O3 -> BN + Al2O3; Al2O3 + SiO2 -> low-melting metakaolinite spinel; Al2O3 + C -> Al2OC + CO

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: Fractography plus XRD/EDS/TEM ties full density and transgranular fracture in HP to an AlN-derived interfacial liquid, and PS porosity to trapped gas

nodes.head: EDS at point A is dominated by Si with a Zr doublet and only small Al, N, C and B peaks. EDS on the HP5 interfacial band shows clear Al with Si and B, C, N, on a Zr-dominated spectrum
nodes.solves: Nano-scale Al-rich, N- and B-bearing glassy layers and a multilayer carbon band wet the ZrB2/SiC boundaries
nodes.note: the text calls the phase 'mainly boron, carbon, silicon and zirconium'; in the panel B and C sit at the noise level while Si is by far the largest peak judge re-read of the F5a spectrum against the keV axis: Zr Lalpha at ~2.05 keV is the largest peak (~55 counts), Al at 1.49 keV is ~22 and Si at 1.74 keV ~12, with B, C and N clear at 10-13 above a noisy baseline. So the panel shows an Al-, N- and B-bearing signal but not an Al-dominated one, and the Zr comes from the surrounding grains in the interaction volume. The text places this N- and B-bearing spectrum in Fig. 6b, but in the image file it belongs to panel (a) (HP5); panel (b) (PS5) is Zr-dominated at ~1100 counts with C ~310 and only ~80 of Al.

F7.caption: Fig. 8. TEM nanographs of HP5 sample, showing the presence of (a) solidified liquid phase between $\mathrm { Z r B } _ { 2 }$ and SiC particles as well as (b) interfacial graphite phase.

use: EDS pattern of such a phase (point A) is presented in Fig. 4a, and indicates the presence of several elements, mainly boron, carbon, silicon and zirconium with small amounts of nitrogen and aluminum.
Also, EDS spectrum of formed glassy phase (Point B) in PS1 sample, which is presented in Fig. 4b, shows different chemical compositions from that observed in HP1 sample (Fig. 4a).
Intragranular fracture mode of the HP5 sample which is clearly visible at Fig. 6a, as mentioned before, indicates the progress of the sintering process.
Also, several layers of amorphous phases are seen in the micrograph (Fig. 6a), especially an extended interfacial layer of the glassy phase which is indicated by thick markers.
TEM nanograph of the formed nanographite phase at the grain boundaries is presented in Fig. 8b, and endorses the presence of graphitized carbon in HP5 sample.
Fig. 3b which presents the fracture surface of the PS0 sample also indicates the occurrence of sintering phenomenon between the particles.

Features such as neck formation and the remaining effects of the departed particles which are marked by thick markers on Fig. 3b and considered as the visual characteristics of the sintered particles, are clearly smaller in size and lower in amount than those seen at HP0 sample.
Also, EDS spectrum of formed glassy phase (Point B) in PS1 sample, which is presented in Fig. 4b, shows different chemical compositions from that observed in HP1 sample (Fig. 4a).
However, the presence of nitrogen and boron elements is clearly visible at the EDS spectrum of the interfacial glassy phase (Fig. 6b), which may be due to the presence of BN at mentioned areas.
In the other side, fracture surface of the PS5 sample which is presented in Fig. 6b, shows several necks formed at the contact areas of particles.
EDS spectrum presented at Fig. 6b indicates the presence of several elements at mentioned phase.

10.1016/j.matchar.2015.10.016#F7a.definition: solidified liquid phase between $\mathrm { Z r B } _ { 2 }$ and SiC particles as well as
use: TEM nanograph of such a solidified amorphous phase is shown in Fig. 8a as a nano-scale interfacial bright layer spread between $\mathrm { Z r B } _ { 2 }$ and SiC grains.
BN peak at the XRD pattern of HP5 sample (Fig. 7a) shows the formation of small amounts of boron nitride, as a result of several chemical reactions occurring during the hot pressing process.

As it can be seen at Fig. 7a, no peak of $\mathrm { \ A l _ { 2 } O _ { 3 } }$ phase is detected by XRD analysis, which endorses the formation of $\mathsf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O } _ { 3 }$ -containing glassy phase during the hot pressing process.
According to the Fig. 7a, no sign of AlN is detected at the XRD pattern of HP5 samples, which indicates that the whole of aluminum nitride additive has been consumed during hot pressing.

Also the XRD pattern of sample PS5 (Fig. 7b), indicates an aluminum oxycarbide phase, $\mathsf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O C }$ . which is more likely to form via the following reaction [41]: The mentioned phase which has a hexagonal crystalline structure and melting point of about $2 4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ [41], may be mixed with amorphous phase and therefore, cannot be morphologically investigated.
The presence of amorphous phase is obvious in XRD pattern presented at Fig. 7b.
Measured relative densities of HP and PS samples are presented in Fig. 2a.
